By Bo Erickson, Susan Heavey and Katharine Jackson WASHINGTON, Sept 25 (Reuters) – US President Donald Trump said on Friday he discussed the Iran war with Chinese President Xi Jinping, as the US ambassador to China said Trump in White House talks made clear that Chinese help for Iran is unacceptable.

“We did,” Trump told reporters when asked whether he talked to Xi about Iran. “I think we’re going to do great.”

The US Ambassador to China David Perdue in a Friday CNBC interview said Trump reiterated to Xi that direct or indirect support for Iran was “totally unacceptable.”

Show Full Article

Asked separately on Fox News if that meant China would stop assisting Iran, Perdue said Washington received assurances from Beijing on Thursday.

“We’ve seen movement … on that already. That’s what the commitment is. They assured us yesterday they’re not doing that,” Perdue told Fox News’ “America’s Newsroom” program.

Trump and Xi did not take formal questions during the three-day state visit to Washington.

Earlier this month, Trump brushed aside a report that Iran acquired satellite images of a base in Jordan from Chinese entities before an attack that killed three US troops there in July.

“They basically do what we do,” Trump told reporters aboard Air Force One on September 13. “When they say China spies on us, I say you’re right and we spy on them too.”

(Reporting by Katharine Jackson, Susan Heavey and Bo Erickson; Editing by Peter Graff, Mark Porter and Chris Reese)

Volkswagen is cutting jobs, closing factories. Why its old business model is breaking

Saptak Datta

25 September, 2026 08:51 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

Volkswagen decided to cut 50,000 jobs worldwide | Liesa Johannssen | Reuters

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

New Delhi: German carmaker Volkswagen has found itself in a fix as the company grapples with multiple crises like slashing profit margins, sweeping global layoffs and the potential winding down of its factories. The automotive giant is undergoing the largest restructuring plan in its 89-year-old history.

On Friday, the CEO of the second-largest automaker got a nod from the stakeholders for the overhaul in the company. However, he is pressured in Germany over job cuts and the firm’s stand of its on-ground strategy in the US.

The company’s supervisory board needs to settle the matter of  Audi’s proposed US production plant—a move that requires clearance from the committee.

Show Full Article

Additionally, the company has also decided to cut 50,000 jobs. The crisis has moved out of Europe and hit China—its most critical and profitable market. In April, Volkswagen eliminated 20,000 Chinese positions, bringing its regional headcount from 90,000 to 70,000 employees. With market demand being slow, the management signalled that further workforce cuts are expected.

“I had hoped that the measures agreed in 2024 would already be sufficient. Unfortunately, that has not been the case,” Volkswagen brand head Thomas Schaefer said . “We have absolutely no time to lose and will therefore significantly step up our performance programme once again. The company and employee representatives will discuss how to proceed.”

‘We cannot escape this trend’ Last week, the second-largest automaker flagged $11.5 billion in financial adjustments, largely driven by struggles at its Porsche brand and a sharp deterioration in the Chinese market. Consequently, it slashed the 2026 operating profit margin forecast to a maximum of 1 per cent.

Apart from Porsche, Volkswagen, which also includes Skoda and Audi, had previously forecasted profit margins between 4 per cent and 5.5 per cent. High tariffs, hard competition in Asia and a declining Chinese market are the three external pressures that have effectively broken Volkswagen’s legacy business model, eroding the premium once commanded by European engineering.

The development illustrates Europe’s struggle as the continent is caught in a high-stakes economic balancing act with both the US and China reshaping global trade through protectionism, industrial subsidies, and geopolitical rivalry.

Volkswagen said a “further deterioration in the market environment, especially in China”, where domestic competitors have eroded its market share. This is compounded by an accelerated demand shift toward electric vehicles (EVs), which remain less profitable for the group than combustion engine models.

Volkswagen’s profit in China has plunged more than 80 per cent in the last 10 years. The company has also fallen behind local Chinese competitors since 2025.

“The world’s largest single market has slumped by 20 per cent, with no consolidation in sight. We cannot escape this trend,” chief financial officer Arno Antlitz said .

Also read: Why is Kedarnath pilgrimage getting harder to manage? 50 tonnes of waste generated in 5 months

‘Most inefficient factories’ Heavy regulatory pressure, structural cost disadvantages, and intensifying global competition have forced Europe’s largest automaker into a historic existential crisis.

“Most managers have failed to keep pace with developments in e-mobility, digitalisation and battery technology, thereby causing the German automotive and supplier industries to fall behind,” said Horst Ott of trade union IG Metall.

Volkswagen is reportedly burning more capital on manufacturing than its competitors. Due to structural issues and rigid labour contracts in Germany, its production facilities are severely underutilised. For instance, factories like Zwickau are projected to drop to just 42 per cent capacity utilisation by 2030, transforming them into massive financial liabilities.

“VW’s (Volkswagen’s) factories are some of the most inefficient I have ever seen,” one of the former executives told Financial Times . “The first time I walked around Wolfsburg properly [VW’s main factory at its headquarters] I was just gobsmacked.”

Striking back against management’s aggressive cost-cutting plans, Volkswagen works council chief Daniela Cavallo and IG Metall union head Christiane Benner demanded stronger protection against unfair Chinese competition. The labour leaders also called for a more effective EU subsidy policy and the continuation of a phased retirement program to protect older workers.

This intervention from Germany’s most powerful labour leaders underscores the friction between corporate leadership, workers, and regional policy.

“We expect corporate leaders and management teams to take responsibility for Germany as an automotive nation, for employees and for jobs,” Benner said.

For decades, Volkswagen’s corporate governance model—which grants workers significant board-level influence—served as a shield against rapid, forced downsizing. However, as the structural realities of the EV transition set in, the traditional social partnership between German labour and corporate executives is fracturing.

Meanwhile, Volkswagen investors are claiming that the company has become self-obsessed and doesn’t focus on manufacturing better cars.

“VW spends too much time on itself, rather than worrying about what it should be hyper-focused on: the Chinese competition,” an investor told The Financial Times .

Can AI produce para-athletes? Finalists from AP, Telangana, Tamil Nadu, Odisha are among young innovators

Samsung Solve for Tomorrow is a global initiative where students use technology to solve community challenges.

Sakshi Mehra

25 September, 2026 06:41 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

File Photo | Kim Hong-Ji | Reuters

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

New Delhi: Eight young innovators from Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Tamil Nadu and Odisha have reached the Top 20 of the Samsung Solve for Tomorrow 2026 competition. They bring five technology-based ideas aimed at improving para-sports, athlete performance, swimming safety and exercise support for people with Parkinson’s disease.

Samsung Solve for Tomorrow is an innovation competition where students use STEM to solve community challenges. In its fifth edition in India, Samsung Solve for Tomorrow has four themes: AI Living for India, Health & Education, Environmental Sustainability, and Sport & Tech.

The eight innovators — Pasupuleti Ruthvik, Kolla Venkata Siva Surya, Homanshika Reddy Pullagurla, Vatala Harika, Ritesh Routray, Manoj Kumar Kasinathan, Jena R and Chriswin William D — are part of a national Top 20 cohort representing 18 cities across 12 states.

Show Full Article

More than half of the finalists come from Tier 2 and Tier 3 cities, Samsung said. The Top 20 teams are now receiving mentorship and support to develop prototypes. Four winning teams will collectively receive Rs 2 crore in grants and incubation support from FITT-IIT Delhi.

Making swimming safer for visually impaired athletes Two of the five projects focus on challenges faced by visually impaired swimmers.

Pasupuleti Ruthvik, 21, from Chittoor developed Untethered, a wearable sensor system designed to alert swimmers when they are approaching the end of a pool lane.

For visually impaired swimmers, reaching the wall without a visual cue can be difficult and may result in head injuries. Ruthvik’s system provides real-time alerts, reducing dependence on manual cues from coaches and allowing swimmers to train more independently.

Kolla Venkata Siva Surya, 16, from Visakhapatnam, is working on a different challenge: maintaining direction inside the lane. His assistive trajectory system detects when a swimmer begins to move away from the intended path and provide real-time feedback, allowing the swimmer to correct their trajectory.

Also Read: Samsung turned first foldable iPhone launch into a roast. Apple fans are hitting back

Using AI to identify para-sport talent In Sundargarh, Vatala Harika, 21, and Ritesh Routray, 20, are using AI to identify para-athletes.

Their project, ParaSync, is an AI-based platform that assesses adaptive sporting techniques and identifies promising athletes. It also aims to connect them with professional coaching and competitive opportunities.

The project is based on the idea that sporting talent can emerge outside established sporting centres, where athletes may have fewer opportunities to access formal training and competition.

Wearables for safer exercise and training In Chennai, Manoj Kumar Kasinathan, 21, Jena R, 20, and Chriswin William D, 20, are developing Rogue, a wearable device aimed at supporting exercise for people with Parkinson’s disease.

In Hyderabad, 21-year-old Homanshika Reddy Pullagurla is developing Somatrace, an IoT-enabled wearable designed to monitor spinal load among precision-sport athletes.

The device tracks movement and physical load in real time, helping athletes understand the strain their bodies experience during training and how they respond to different movements.

The eight innovators took part in a prototyping programme with FITT-IIT Delhi that included an Innovation Bootcamp and online mentoring from Samsung experts.

The programme helped them understand users’ needs, develop prototypes, identify potential markets, and understand the impact and scalability of their ideas.

They also visited Samsung Design Delhi, Samsung R&D Institute India facilities in Noida, Delhi, and Bengaluru, and Samsung’s headquarters in Gurugram.

Now in its fifth edition in India, Samsung Solve for Tomorrow has four themes: AI Living for India, Health & Education, Environmental Sustainability, and Sport & Tech.

Opinion

Why the Trump-Xi summit just produced a truce, not a breakthrough

The Donald Trump-Xi Jinping Summit is best understood as the TRUCE, shaping a bipolar international system amid its multipolar pushbacks.

Swasti Rao

25 September, 2026 04:47 pm IST

2

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping | (c) Copyright Thomson Reuters 2025

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

T he pageantry in Washington was elaborate enough to make the Donald Trump-Xi Jinping summit look like a G2 truce. Trump personally received Xi at Joint Base Andrews. US aircraft such as B-2s and F-22s flew overhead, military bands marched, the White House rolled out a state dinner, Trump made Xi laugh and eventually discovered that the Chinese president shared his appreciation for one particular American asset: “ h e loves good granite”.

Strip away the granite, however, and a simpler question emerges: what kind of TRUCE did this truce actually achieve?

The answer can be decoded rather neatly by turning the word into an acronym.

Show Full Article

T for trade truce extended.

R for reciprocal leverage retained — Chinese rare earths versus American technology controls.

U for an unsettled Taiwan.

C for competition contained, not concluded.

E for engagement expanded, particularly on artificial intelligence (AI) , without much new institutional architecture.

TRUCE captures both change and continuity and shows the limits of G2. Washington and Beijing have bought themselves more stability, but they did not dismantle the instruments with which they compete or resolve the bottlenecks that engulf their strategic interests .

T: Trade truce, extended—not reinvented The conversation around the economic truce did not begin at the current summit.

Its immediate foundations were laid when Trump and Xi met in Busan, South Korea, on 30 October 2025, following months of tariff escalation. Under the arrangement implemented from 10 November in the same year , Washington suspended its heightened reciprocal tariffs on China for one year while retaining a 10 per cent reciprocal tariff. It also cut 10 percentage points from tariffs imposed over fentanyl flows.

China, meanwhile, reciprocated by suspending retaliatory tariffs and several non-tariff measures, easing restrictions involving rare earths and critical minerals, resuming purchases of American agricultural commodities and tightening controls on fentanyl precursors.

The Busan arrangement was due to expire on 10 November this year . As Xi arrived in Washington, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced that the truce would now continue until 10 January 2027.

This is where American political scientist Rush Doshi’s pre-summit checklist becomes quite useful to revisit. He argued that the duration of any extension would tell us something about the relationship itself. Beijing wanted a much longer period of stability while Washington preferred a shorter extension, partly because the US remained dissatisfied with Chinese compliance, particularly over critical-mineral supplies.

The outcome suggests quite convincingly that neither side wanted escalation, but Washington was unwilling to lock itself into détente in the guise of stability.

Also read: India-China reset has limits. Don’t mistake it for a boundary settlement — see Taksing

R: Reciprocal leverage retained Doshi’s more provocative argument concerned China’s changing leverage.

Beijing, he had argued before the summit, believes its ability to squeeze rare-earth supplies has altered Washington’s calculations. The present phase —  what he calls a “détente but not quite a détente” — suits the Chinese narrative that thinks time may increasingly favour it in the larger competition.

One need not accept that conclusion in entirety to see what has changed. Let me explain.

For decades, discussions of economic interdependence assumed that America’s advantages lay in technology and finance while China’s vulnerabilities lay in access to markets and advanced innovation. That part of the relationship is now considerably more reciprocal.

China has shown the geopolitical value of its dominance in critical-mineral processing. But Washington continues to wield formidable advantages through advanced semiconductor and technology controls.

During the current summit, neither has surrendered that leverage. Beijing’s official statement speaks of a “new joint arrangement” between the economic teams, but gives no dramatic new tariff concessions or the abandonment of Chinese critical-mineral leverage. It does not mention any major American relaxation of advanced-technology controls either.

Importantly, Beijing has released detailed official accounts of the summit in both Chinese and English. At the time of writing, there is no joint statement or a comparable detailed post-summit account from the White House. The Chinese version therefore provides the fullest available official account of the closed-door exchanges, but it cannot, by itself, establish what Washington agreed to.

The summit therefore did not conclude this coercive interdependence. It, however, established more political space for managing it.

That is a subtle but an important takeaway. US-China strategic stability increasingly depends not on resolving economic weaponisation, but on both realising how to manage the escalation around it.

Also read: Chinese commentary on Xi-Trump summit is a cross between flowers and daggers

U: Unsettled Taiwan Taiwan, once again, offers the clearest evidence of the limits of this new stability.

Xi asked Washington to accept what Beijing called their position of “opposing Taiwan independence.” The key phrase in Mandarin is fandui Taidu — literally, oppose Taiwan independence.

Washington’s established formulation has been close but not identical. It says that the US does not support Taiwan independence. Beijing would prefer something stronger but which Washington does not endorse.

Experts specifically said that semantics would be one of the tests worth watching.

Yet Beijing’s own statement records Xi making the demand without mentioning that the US accepted it.

Continued ambiguity on Taiwan, therefore, matters as much as subtle changes in Trump’s overall rhetoric to respect Beijing’s position. Once again, this deliberate word play remains a part of the broader management, not a conclusive position on their most dangerous fault line.

Trump’s uncertainty can itself have strategic consequences. But so far there is no evidence that Washington formally shifted to Beijing’s preferred formulation on Taiwan.

Also read: Trump’s Greenland deal changes little. His bullying can change US-Denmark ties

C: Competition contained — and Beijing wants a Naamkaran This is the most interesting part of the summit.

In May, Trump and Xi agreed in Beijing to pursue what both governments called a “constructive US-China relationship of strategic stability.” The White House itself used a closely matching phrase in its May fact sheet.

It is worth pausing here because “strategic stability” used by the US  traditionally carries a narrower, almost Cold War nuance — nuclear deterrence, escalation control and preventing catastrophic conflict between major powers.

Xi’s formulation is much broader. China’s official explanation describes constructive strategic stability as a relationship in which cooperation is the mainstay, competition remains within proper limits, differences are manageable, and peace can be expected. In other words, cooperate where possible, compete without losing control, manage what cannot be resolved, and prevent the rivalry from escalating to war.

The phrase, therefore, does not mean an absence of competition and seeks to define the acceptable boundaries of competition.

And Beijing clearly wants to institutionalise it. Xi’s statement said the two sides should now turn this vision “into action”. He wants engagement between ministries, economic officials, militaries and other institutions to thicken.

This is why I would distinguish constructive strategic stability, the actual agreed-upon phrase, from the looser idea of “comprehensive strategic stability”. Beijing’s ambition may indeed be comprehensive — extending beyond traditional military stability into economics, technology and political behaviour — but it is still not the terminology both governments officially adopted in May.

Once again, the difference in approach between Xi and Trump becomes telling.

Edgard Kagan, former US Ambassador to Malaysia , and now at the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), has also drawn attention to the importance of the relationship between the two leaders and the differences in how they approach the bilateral relationship. I would frame it as Trump personalises, but Xi institutionalises.

Trump speaks the language of friendship, deals and leader-to-leader chemistry and uses Trumpian pick-up lines to further his style of diplomacy. Xi speaks of frameworks, limits, departments, mechanisms and the formal relationship between two major powers.

Also read: How China sees US calls for AI slowdown. Its companies now get more room to catch up

E: Engagement expands—but does it ‘thicken’? AI may provide the best test here.

Before the summit, Bessent had already hailed emerging US-China AI discussions, and officials were exploring something more ambitious: communication mechanisms dealing with serious AI incidents and national-security risks.

Doshi, therefore, posed an excellent question before Xi arrived: would this dialogue become “thick” or remain “thin”?

If it indeed thickens — w ould agencies engage regularly? Would mechanisms survive political tensions? In a genuine emergency, would someone actually pick up the phone and make a call?

Washington Summit provided only a partial answer at best.

Xi proposed continuing AI dialogue, discussing both risks and benefits, preventing misuse and ensuring that artificial intelligence remains under human control. Trump, according to the Chinese statement, supported continued dialogue and cooperation.

But no genuine AI-safety regime emerged, and neither did any major bilateral mechanism come out. Trump has resisted imposing additional restraints on AI development, while Xi’s language repeatedly stresses human control.

So engagement has expanded enough for headlines, but its institutional architecture remains thin.

Also read: New India-US trade portal shows India is trying to liberalise and protect at the same time

More than spectacle, less than settlement This brings us back to Washington’s pageantry.

Reporting by Reuters described a meeting heavy on symbolism but light on breakthroughs across trade, Taiwan, AI and Iran.¹³ The Financial Times had anticipated pretty much the same logic before the talks, ie Xi’s central objective was to consolidate the more stable environment established since Busan and Beijing, rather than pin its success on headline-grabbers.¹⁴

There were continuities elsewhere too. One did not see any major new military crisis-management mechanism. Iran, Ukraine and the Korean Peninsula were discussed without producing breakthroughs. Beijing’s statement expectedly does not record a significant outcome on detainees or human rights.⁶

Yet calling the summit inconsequential because the deliverables were thin would miss its larger importance where due.

Trump and Xi appear to have moved from repeatedly asking whether their rivalry can be resolved to how a rivalry that cannot be resolved can be managed.

That is where constructive strategic stability and lack of unending breakthroughs become reassuring, even if with a hint of discomfort.

Uncomfortable, because the concept could also become a vehicle through which each tries to constrain the other’s behaviour. Seeking strategic stability cannot be indefinitely politically neutral.

Also read: The India-China reset will be tested in the Northeast

The bipolar ceiling above a multipolar world There is one reason why the Washington summit matters.

Writing in The Indian Express ahead of the summit, C Raja Mohan argued that multilateral institutions, however ambitious, operate within parameters set by great-power politics rather than independently determining the international order.

The Xi-Trump summit happened as leaders from across the world gathered around the United Nations, trying to assert their agency and space in the era of growing unpredictability.

At the granular level, the contemporary international system increasingly looks multipolar. Middle powers have become more active. New plurilaterals have proliferated — the latest being the Partners for Multilateralism that Canada floated with the EU, India, Brazil, Kenya, Australia and Barbados on board.

India, Europe, Japan, Australia and the Gulf states have been developing overlapping strategic partnerships. These middle-power initiatives promise issue-based cooperation outside traditional great-power blocs.

Yet the world’s most consequential strategic questions continue operating in an oddly bipolar world.

Whichever way the elusive G2 is defined, neither Washington nor Beijing can simply dictate outcomes to others. But they continue to shape an extraordinary portion of the international system’s grand strategic boundaries.

Therefore, the Washington truce is best understood as the TRUCE, shaping a bipolar international system amid its multipolar pushback.

Swasti Rao is a Consulting Editor (International and Strategic Affairs) at ThePrint. She tweets @swasrao. Views are personal.
